blocks.text: Electron-withdrawing groups such as a halogen atom have a negative inductive effect (-I). The halogen withdraws the bonded electrons from the carbon-carbon bond and so displays a negative inductive effect; this causes a permanent dipole in the molecule in which the halogen atom holds a negative charge and the carbon becomes partially positive (Figure 11.12). The electron-deficient C1 then pulls electrons from the C1-C2 bond, so C2 carries a smaller positive charge than C1.

blocks.alt: Chain C-C-C-C-Cl with the carbons numbered 4, 3, 2, 1 in red. Red chevrons on the C2-C1 bond (three) and the C1-Cl bond (four) point towards Cl. Charges: delta-delta+ on C2, delta+ on C1, delta- on Cl. Labels: Less positive charge than C1 (arrow onto C2); Less electronegative (C1); More electronegative (Cl); Electron deficient C1 pulling electrons from C1-C2 covalent bond (arrow onto the C2-C1 bond).
blocks.caption: Figure 11.12: Inductive effect: Polarization of sigma bond (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.12).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed Figure 11.12 marks both C1 and C2 'delta++'. As the book's text says, C2 carries a smaller positive charge than C1: delta+ on C1 and delta-delta+ on C2, as drawn above.
